Ian Thurston  

This book is the final part of a trilogy on the subject of political morality, in the course of which Coline Covington brings together her vast experience not only of psychoanalysis but also of conflict resolution and group relations. Although a sober subject—a critique of the concept of collective guilt—it is written with characteristic style and panache as she creatively negotiates the difficult task of interweaving perspectives from the clinical setting, social research, historical studies, film and literature, and from the Judeo-Christian tradition from which secular concepts of guilt, responsibility and atonement largely derive. Giving examples from conflicts across the world ranging from the Balkans, Sierra Leonne, Rwanda, Sri Lanka and Nazi Germany the spirit of the work is that of trying as best as possible to face reality rather than seeing things as we feel they should be, and of falling prey to the moralistic fallacy.

She begins with a brief personal account of moving as a child with her family from the deep south of America to New York City and thus having to relinquish her relationship with her beloved nanny Beulah. She recalls a pervasive homesickness, a sense of a lost Eden, of displacement and dislocation. She conveys the contrast between the complexities and contradictions of actual historical identifications, such as those connected to the legacy of the American Civil war, and the way in which public rituals of remembrance based on notions of guilt, atonement and restitution tends to offer a dichotomous view of good and bad, righteous and profane. The author's parents came from what had been slave-owning families. She comments that while they never voiced personal guilt they did, as lifelong campaigners for civil rights and racial equality, take responsibility—a distinction which is central to the book.

The author stresses the clinical importance of bearing witness, validating personal experience, helping the client put traumatic experience into words, thus becoming more able to detach from self-blame and destructive relational dynamics; processes for which there are socio-political correlates, not least the importance of public acknowledgement of injustice, recalling the German chancellor Wily Brandt falling on his knees to apologize for the Warsaw ghetto. She cautions, however, that whilst such acknowledgements may help some victims, there is mixed evidence at best for their impact on the larger society. She necessarily reminds us that it is the political context within which rituals of remembrance and atonement take place which might determine their ultimate meaning and effectiveness, and that without the presence of effective legal structures, civic equality and basic security, they may have limited impact—or even be counterproductive.

Measuring outcomes can be a divisive subject within the counselling and psychotherapy professions with many practitioners either reporting that it is irrelevant to their daily practice, at odds with their theoretical approach or too difficult to engage with and understand. Evans and Carlyle, however, challenge these positions in their introductory textbook on outcome measures (OMs) and evaluation in counselling and psychotherapy, and have produced a step-by-step, practice-oriented guide which aims to demystify several misconceptions about using OMs in clinical practice. They have written a practical, user-friendly and balanced book primarily aimed at individual practitioners, service managers, supervisors and health professionals working with clients within mental health settings (although there is much here that would be of interest and value to researchers and academics, especially those early in their careers).

One of the book's many appeals is its accessibility, and how both authors have translated their not-so-insignificant experience as practitioner-researchers into an insightful, down-to-earth read without dumbing down the topic, or overwhelming the reader with impenetrable research jargon. Although the book is inclusive of all therapeutic modalities, both authors trained analytically and much of what they discuss and propose in the book speaks to their clinical backgrounds and will be of importance to psychoanalytic, psychodynamic and Jungian practitioners on a general level. There is, however, some psychodynamic focus in the book, including a useful case study of a psychodynamic therapist (called Jan) who explores how she might incorporate OMs into her analytic practice for the first time and how she hopes OMs will enhance her work. The authors also highlight some measures that are specific to the psychodynamic model, including the Depressive Experiences Questionnaire, Defense Style Questionnaire, Quality of Object Relations, Attachment Measures and Shedler-Westen Assessment Procedure (SWAP). However, given the book's broad approach, you may be left wondering what does this book really offer those practitioners working psychodynamically? Joel Paris (2019) has described how, despite a growing evidence base, psychodynamic therapies have continued to decline. He attributes this decline to the idea that psychodynamic therapies overall are not as fully committed as other modalities to the principles of evidence-based practice (although this situation is much improved and improving—see British Psychoanalytic Council Evidence Base1), and that psychodynamic therapies are generally less open to interdisciplinary perspectives and transtheoretical models. By writing a general textbook, the authors have drawn on lessons from across different psychotherapy modalities and have kept an eye to the broader trends within the counselling and psychotherapy professions in relation to OMs and evaluation. The book, therefore, provides a guide on how the ideas and methods of different orientations (including psychodynamic) can contribute to a more pluralistic approach and understanding. The authors have placed learning about OMs into a wider context, offering tools and principles for measuring clinical practice with a range of issues common to all modalities, including depression, anxiety, interpersonal relationships and setting goals. To differentiate the Social Dreaming Matrix from Group Relations Conferences, Gordon Lawrence provided a specific denomination, framework and primary task. Despite these new parameters, Lawrence understood that group dynamics persisted in the Matrix, perceiving social dreaming and group dynamics as two lenses of a binocular informing the Matrix. However, to fulfil the Matrix's primary task of accessing the social unconscious, he advocated a non-psychoanalytic monocular vision emphasizing social dreaming. In this article, I argue that the Social Dreaming Matrix and the Dream Reflection Dialogue that follows are, from a psychoanalytic perspective, two moments of a group whose primary task is Social Dreaming. Looking from a psychoanalytic perspective through the two lenses of social dreaming and group dynamics provides a wider perspective of the social unconscious, generating insights. This group psychoanalytic approach is a found-and-created framework rediscovering and recreating the object-Social Dreaming Matrix framework proposed by Lawrence. To support this argument, I analysed a series of Social Dreaming Matrixes and Dream Reflection Dialogues occurring during a social dreaming training programme to show how the unfolding group dynamics revealed the social unconscious as did social dreaming.

The technical aspect of managing the analyst's emotional responses to a patient has changed over the years, from Freud's position (1910, 1912, 1915), stating that emotions are a sign of an incomplete analysis from the analyst, to the recognition of this emotion as a communication between patient and analyst by Bion (1954). This recognition led to the acknowledgment of their importance as a diagnostic tool, while avoiding disclosure by Heiman (1950) and King (1978). More recently, consideration in the ways we can interpret these feelings during the analysis has been study (Winnicott, 1947; Little 1951; Casement 1986; Ogden 2018). This paper, advocates for the disclosure of such feelings (self-disclosure) mainly when they are of a positive nature and the patient has a history of neglect. Also, there is a reflection on the advantages and disadvantages of doing so. Finally, there is consideration of the difference between a patient's need and a patient's desire before such disclosures.

Anne Zachary  

The first thing to clarify in my review is that this book has nothing to do with the recent crisis about abortion in the USA. The US Supreme court overturned women's right to abortion in Roe v Wade, which was reported around the world as a very 401 backward step. The reader might think from the title that it is then about the modern technologies now available in the field of fertility, conception and childbirth. These are mentioned of course in Part Two with a good summary of what is available (pp. 77-9). But the book is actually a psychoanalytic exploration of the consequences of these new technological realities.

It is prefaced by a review of the psychoanalytic theory of sexuality in Part One. Originally published in Italian, it is beautifully translated by Adam Elgar. There are three words to mention that stand out in the book, perhaps with a note of ‘tongue in cheek’ to lighten a complex and controversial subject. The first is ‘Scandal’, to be explored a little later. The second is ‘Caesura’, the word for a break in a line of poetry to allow for taking a breath, and the third, ‘Excursus’, which onomatopoeic enough in meaning, describes that line (comprising the whole of Part One), which is actually 79 pages long! If it is a criticism, because it will completely take the reader's mind away from the main controversial focus of the book, the new biotechnologies, it is a very small one because that particular ‘line’ is such a useful and indepth revision of the Oedipus-centred, primal scene based, Freudian theory of sexuality in itself.

In Part One, be prepared to revise Freud on sexuality. The chapters are entitled, ‘The return of the repressed’ and ‘The world of yesterday: end of innocence’; the latter about presenting ‘Beyond the pleasure principle’ to austere, respectable Vienna. In this chapter, Freud's case histories, little Hans and Dora, are revisited. Then, Chapter 3, the perversions, infantile sexuality and puberty, and Freud's (1905) ‘3 essays on sexuality’. Chapter 4 is entitled ‘Time in sexuality’, an essay coursing around Ferenczi's (1949) ‘Confusion of the tongues between the adults and the child: the language of tenderness and of passion’. Part One is the ‘Excursus’ and does not disappoint.

Catriona Wrottesley  

Just over a decade ago, psychoanalyst Mark Gerald (2011), undertook a project entitled, 'In the Shadow of Freud's Couch: Portraits of Psychoanalysts in their 404 Offices'. Having made photographic portraits of more than 50 analysts in their offices he concluded that

these professional offices were often so much more than simply a work space. They were a created area in which the deepest wishes and darkest fears could be revealed, held and explored. These rooms were houses for the unconscious world and, as such, typically remained outside of the realm of awareness, being as important as they were … What is it about a psychoanalytic office? How connected, even merged, are we and our patients with these spaces? (Gerald, 2011, p. 436).

The meaning that patients and analysts bestow the room space and the objects therein are often deeply personal. More recently, psychoanalyst Alessandra Lemma (2020) has written about how patients relate to the analyst's physicality or the physical space of the consulting room to connect with ‘an as yet unrealized and wished-for embodied self’ (p. 57) that can only be experienced by identifying with aspects of the analyst's body or of the consulting room. Child therapist Tami Pollak (2022) has written about the body and the consulting room's materiality as a path for developing intersubjective psychophysical space. Positioning a lens over a specific area in these ways enables more to be seen.

Just so, Debbie Wright's recent book enables new and detailed ways of viewing and thinking about the concrete, metaphorical and transferential dimensions of the therapist's workspace, an important and under-developed subject. Whatever and wherever the space in which therapy takes place, it is subject to projections of meaning for patients and therapists, often provoked by the presence and absence of objects, marks, textures, smells, dimensionality, and emotional atmospheres and triggers.

Wright is a psychotherapist and academic in the Department of Psychosocial and Psychoanalytic Studies at the University of Essex, and also an artist, illustrator and printmaker. Her wide-ranging interests furnish us with unique perspectives and her book explodes with ideas. To illuminate her thesis, she adopts an inter-disciplinary approach, drawing on object relations theory, art, history, philosophy, anthropology and archaeology, and includes disparate settings including that of Neanderthals and early Hominins, Nigerian village life, Westminster Abbey, residential care settings, psychotherapy consulting rooms and the virtual space of the psychotherapy consulting room, before turning her attention to the novels of E.M. Forster. Throughout, the book is richly illustrated by Wright's own drawings and those of Sigmund Freud. Chapter 2, ‘Spatialisation and rooms’, is devoted to Sigmund Freud. Freud's drawings include one of his room in ‘Zoologische Station’ in Trieste, 1876, another of his table in that consulting room, a letter to Eduard Silberstein dated 5 April 1876, showing Freud's drawings of his desk and chair, and various drawings he had made of the brain's workings.

Danny Taggart   Senior Lecturer and Academic Director of the Clinical Psychology Doctorate at the University of Essex. From 2019 to 2022 he worked as Clinical Lead and Principal Psychologist to the Truth Project at the Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse. He continues to work with child abuse inquiry legacy projects across the United Kingdom and with survivor groups.

The knowledge of child sexual abuse (CSA)—the recognition of its prevalence and the reality of its impact—has been lost and found in repeated cycles within society and perhaps particularly within the field of mental health. A recent compendium published by the Office for National Statistics (ONS, 2019) provides an estimate of the prevalence of CSA. It found that one in 13 adults reported experiencing CSA, with 9% in total reporting contact CSA and 3% non-contact CSA. This represents a population level estimate of 3.1 million adults having experienced CSA in the UK.

The long-term health and social impacts of CSA are significant. In adulthood, victims and survivors of CSA are at elevated risk of an interlocking, aggregated triad of psychological, physical and social injuries (Taggart et al., 2021). These include increased exposure to a range of mental health conditions; depression (Salokangas et al. 2020), anxiety disorders (Heim & Nemeroff, 2001), psychosis (Shevlin, Dorachy & Adamson, 2007), dissociative disorders (Chu & Dill, 1990), in addition to complex post-traumatic stress disorder (C-PTSD) and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) (Cloitre & Ford, 2016). There is also increased risk of chronic physical health conditions, including respiratory conditions (Bellis et al., 2014), diabetes (Huffhines, Noser & Patton, 2016) and premature death (Happell et al, 2017). In addition to health outcomes, there are also significant social impairments caused by CSA, including difficulties engaging with public services (Mason, Taggart & Broadhurst, 2020) and betrayal trauma (Freyd, 1996). There are social and economic costs to wider society—a recent UK study estimated that efforts linked to prevention, lost economic output, the overall health and criminal justice costs amounted to £10.1 billion in the year 2018-19 (Radakin et al., 2021).

The Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse (IICSA) was established as a statutory Inquiry in England and Wales in 2015. It was commissioned by the then Home Secretary following several high-profile cases of CSA that involved failures in public institutions such as the police, NHS, religious institutions and parliament. IICSA is part of a wave of international Historical Institutional Abuse (HIA) Inquiries 419

SOCIAL INEQUALITY, NHS TALKING THERAPIES, ACTIVISM, CLASS, MENTAL HEALTH CRISIS, COMMUNITY PSYCHOTHERAPY

I argue here that we psychotherapists in the private sector bear our own share of responsibility for the institutionalization of a two-tier system of psychological care and therapy. We are on aggregate a profession of the self-employed, focused on the self-development of the individual who can afford to pay our fees. As a profession we appear to be relatively blind to the living conditions of the less well-off citizens in our society and to the ethics of collective responsibility.

Joanna Ryan

Joanna Ryan

London
joannaryan@runbox.com

Joanna Ryan  

This book is a monograph of passionate critique concerning the forms of misogyny to be found embedded in various psychoanalytic concepts, theories, practices and institutions. The book's brevity, Michaela Chamberlain says, is to render it 398 accessible to anyone with an interest in psychoanalysis. It is welcome to have a renewed focus on misogyny and to be reminded once again of its persistence and insidiousness. Chamberlain suggests that misogyny is internalized by both men and women, forming a ‘misogynistic introject’ (p. 56), which is passed through generations of psychoanalysts via the teachings and trainings: ‘It engenders entitlement in male psychoanalysts and shame and otherness in female psychoanalysts’ (p. 56).

Throughout, Chamberlain makes creative use of examples drawn from the work of women artists, especially those who use their own bodies as the artwork. She writes: ‘Women are punished for the desire that men have for them …’ (p. 22), and too often this is accompanied by the male need for control over women, as a denial of their own dependence. Abuse and physical violence are the more extreme forms of misogynistic hatred, some of which have been written about from a psychoanalytic viewpoint. Here the kind of psychoanalytic misogyny Chamberlain sees as perpetuated against women is to be found in theories—something we might construe as symbolic violence—and in practice, in the many uncomfortable and discriminatory but familiar experiences that she illustrates in personal and clinical anecdotes. She also describes the frequent splitting of women's sexuality from their supposed maternal and nurturing capacities.

Chamberlain mainly takes aim at Freudian theory, arguing that misogyny is inherent right from the start in classical and contemporary formulations of the Oedipus complex and in theories of female psychosexual development that are based on differences seen as inferiority, lack or deficit. She briefly mentions the many feminist critiques, from Karen Horney onwards to the recent past, that have been made of such theory. She claims that the various innovative reformulations of female development and sexuality that have been put forward by critical writers such as Jessica Benjamin, Juliet Mitchell, Susie Orbach and many others (all different from each other) have had little impact on what she calls ‘the mainstream’. Rather, she says, these have been side-lined into their own ‘bubbles’, or into alternative institutions. This book is quite explicitly not intended to address any of these works, and it would be a different kind of book if it did. However, many of these writings do attempt to put forward psychoanalytic theories which are not misogynistic and which address women's desires, sexualities, bodies and experiences, phenomena that Chamberlain rightly says are often ignored or misunderstood in many contemporary practices. Her focus only on critique of what is construed as the ‘mainstream’ lends a rather pessimistic feel that I question is completely warranted of psychoanalysis as a whole, though it depends where you look and what is construed as ‘mainstream’, which is not adequately spelled out—or indeed what is deemed ‘proper’ psychoanalysis and by whom.

Emma Letley

emma.letley1@gmail.com

Emma Letley  

This first full-length psychological study of the Dutch-American painter concentrates initially on de Kooning's well-known and controversial series of Woman images of the 1950s and attends to the search for meaning of these. Taylor has, amongst many advantages, that of not being tied to any particular school and is able to traverse a range of commentators and analysts of different modalities.

In Chapter 1, he focuses on Woman I and offers the reader a variety of conflicting responses to the piece, its technique and mood. Only occasional reviewers remarked on the humour of the piece and an element of caricature. Most male critics linked the Woman images to sexual violence. Dora Ashton was the first female critic to offer a positive response, stressing an aesthetic and humanistic interpretation.

Taylor also addresses here de Kooning's response to those critics, accusing him of misogyny, violence and attacking the female form. In the 1960s, de Kooning insisted that he meant the 1950s paintings to be ‘funny’, ‘satiric’ and ‘monstrous’. One early critic, Thomas Hess (1968), noted that the women were likely linked to the artist's mother who had traumatized his childhood. Later critics argued against the interpretation of misogyny whilst a challenge to the feminist view came with the remarks of Fionna Barber (1999), who suggested, convincingly, that the female figure in Woman I shows a ‘body in progress: one that is embodied through the slow additive means of brush on to canvas …’ (p. 41).

Chapter 2 continues the search for meanings, looking at the view of some non-clinical commentators. There are Jungian and Freudian perspectives here, and an extended section on the work of Marlene Clark (2020) (drawing more on object relations theory), who believes that the Woman pieces should be read as ‘self-representational rather than self-biographical’ (p. 65), whilst in her view de Kooning created the Woman as comical images. She emphasizes the strong aspect of self-portraiture in the series, proposing that he puts some aspect of himself into each one.

Julian Lousada  

This is a book about the application of psychoanalytic and systemic ideas to the understanding of group and organization dynamics, including our own contribution, whether as members or ‘consultants’, to the dynamics that unfold. The book is unexpected because it largely omits to mention the rich history of ideas that inform it. Instead, 411 Anton Obholzer conveys a belief that the ideas in the book are not foreign or esoteric, or humourless, but are accessible to us all through experience and observation.

It is a wonderfully personal book predicated as it is on Obholzer's long experience and interest in the life and work of organizations, brought to life in the many examples that pepper the text. The themes of leadership and the exercise of authority are central, but importantly Obholzer's approach is as sensitive as it is thoughtful. He empathizes that he is not offering a template for those in leadership or those who consult, rather he insists that his purpose is to ‘attempt to help create a symbolic tailored’ garment which suits each ‘personal and organisational need’ (p. 5). Not a tailor made but a garment flexible enough to suit responding to what is organizationally needed and fits the person who wears it. Obholzer conveys an inherently respectful stance in which organizational difficulties are not met with judgement or knowing what do, but a curiosity which leads to a shared discovery. This approach is illustrated in the following way when he writes that ‘putting oneself in someone else's shoes, requires us take our shoes off’ (p. 6), and this involves respecting the need that all good work requires, namely that the leader, coach or consultant needs to be in contact with their own creative and flawed selves. Curiosity is a precondition for the tolerance necessary to understand the strengths and flaws of those being led or those we seek to help and work with. Simply put, this book offers itself in the belief that the ideas within it are capable of being available and useful to all. Obholzer's thesis is that these are not privileged ideas available only in the laboratory of the professional but to all who are curious about the vicissitude of organizational life. In this sense, the book has a very welcome and democratic stance. The book demonstrates that the unconscious is ever present and not something to be feared, nor is it essentially unknowable, but rather it presents all who are willing to consider its presence with data that can be useful for learning and action.

SUPERVISION, FUTURE ORIENTATION, EXISTENTIALISM, AUTHENTICITY, CONTINUOUS TEMPORALITY

While exploring the supervisee's implicit contribution to therapeutic interactions, the supervisor can focus on the supervisee's future orientation instead of exploring transference manifestations that might arouse the supervisee's anxiety. I suggest that future orientation is shaped by an implicit urge described in the analytic literature as an unconscious hope to elicit yearned-for psychological nutrients from the environment. In parallel, existentialist literature describes an urge to exercise the freedom to live an authentic life and actualize fundamental personal projects, sometimes against cultural and societal convictions and conventions. Furthermore, frustrating the urge that shapes future orientation might lead to a limited situational crisis described differently by the two schools of thought. While reconstructing the supervisee's therapeutic experiences, the supervisor can discern this urge in the components or response patterns of the supervisee's situational crisis. I will suggest that the supervisory dyad's capacity to formulate the implicit urge that shapes the supervisee's future orientation creates a continuous temporality and enlivens the supervisory and therapeutic processes.

PSYCHOANALYTIC PSYCHOTHERAPY, DEPRESSION, SUICIDE ATTEMPT, LOST LOVE OBJECT, SYMBOLIZATION OF DESIRE

Deborah was referred to me for psychoanalytic psychotherapy following a suicide attempt and depression. We began a fascinating journey spanning more than 10 years. During therapy, many questions arose concerning the suicidal episode, which she could not register consciously. I tried to understand the reasons for her depression and the attempted suicide through the unconscious process in the therapeutic relationship and through the music and poetry that she brought to sessions. In this paper I describe the process of listening for the signifiers of semiotic and symbolic language, both metaphoric and metonymic, as revealed in poetry and music according to the theories of Kristeva and Lacan. The poetry enabled the patient to retrieve childhood memories, experience the movement from unconscious to conscious, and mourn through the experience of transference and countertransference in the therapeutic relationship. Also illustrated is the transition from singing the music to more symbolic language, turning the patient's sensory experience into language, and connecting her personal experience with the culture of her past. The patient's mourning and the lost love objects are discussed through the prism of classical and object relations theories.

SELF-DISCLOSURE, CROSS-THEORETICAL APPROACHES, CREATIVITY, ARTISTRY, IMPROVISATION, WALLERSTEIN, FAIRBAIRN, STOLOROW

This article explores four primary themes while describing the author's process of advising patients of an imminent open-heart surgery: the lingering controversies surrounding self-disclosure, the artistry involved in sharing the information, the management of specific patient reactions, and how the dance between static and dynamic theory application in psychoanalytic psychotherapy unfolds. The author tailored his description of the medical crisis to the distinctiveness of each psychotherapeutic dyad—using a basically scripted but short description of the situation—and he improvised subsequent clinical discussions accordingly. Several patients reacted in surprising ways. Three clinical examples vividly illustrate the above-noted themes, particularly the uniqueness of each dyad, the need for improvisation, and the application of a cross-theoretical model (Karbelnig, 2022).

The forced move to online work in 2020 was initially greeted with consternation by many in the psychoanalytic world, but adaptation was subsequently accomplished by many with successful results for clients. At WPF Therapy where individual psychodynamic psychotherapy is offered by therapists in training, we did a qualitative and participative study with clients, trainees and supervisors to explore how these groups felt about online work. A participative and pluralistic approach was chosen to achieve a fidler and more balanced understanding. Eighteen trainees interviewed each other, 19 supervisors contributed through focus groups and individual interviews, and eight clients’ perspectives were explored in individual interviews. The findings were that working online offered different and exciting opportunities for therapy, including the unconscious processes which are central to the psychodynamic modality. This has implications for future psychodynamic training since new phenomena need to be incorporated into psychoanalytic thinking and practice. While results did not support replacing in-person therapy, there was support for a combined approach in future. As one participant said: ‘The genie's out of the bottle now ’, something has happened which cannot be stopped.

BOARDING SCHOOL, BOARDING SCHOOL SURVIVORS, CHILD DEVELOPMENT, CHILD WELFARE, IDENTITY, MENTAL HEALTH, PSYCHOTHERAPY

This paper aims to consolidate existing literature on the psychological impact of sending children away to boarding schools in Britain. A scarcity of literature pertaining specifically to independent boarding schools leads the author to examine child developmental theory, peer victimization in the British Army, trauma within captivity and adaptive behaviours. In conclusion, it is clear from this research that more time and effort is needed to understand the psychological impact of sending children away from home to be schooled, socialized and parented institutionally. In particular, the ethos and traditions associated with British and colonial schools, and the way in which these things are preserved warrants further study as it appears to be a significant source of the attitude toward children in boarding schools. The psychoanalytic community may be best placed to understand, and make understood, the positive or negative impact on children attending boarding schools in Britain.

Monica Luci

mluci@essex.ac.uk

Monica Luci   Clinical psychologist, Jungian and relational psychoanalyst, and lecturer at the Department of Psychosocial and Psychoanalytic Studies of University of Essex. She is member of the Center for Trauma, Asylum and Refugees of the same university. She has been working for more than 20 years as clinical psychologist, researcher and psychotherapist with vulnerable asylum seekers, especially survivors of torture, human trafficking, gender-based violence and unaccompanied minors in mental health services and NGOs. She teaches in professional courses, and analytic training within the International Association for Analytical Psychology and is author, translator and editor of publications on the themes of trauma, torture, displacement, collective violence, gender, human rights violations and psychoanalysis.
SOUL, HUMAN RIGHTS VIOLATIONS, ANALYTICAL PSYCHOLOGY, REFLECTIVE TRIANGLE, MONOLITHIC SELF STATES, PARADOXICAL MULTIPLE SELF STATES, TORTURE, GENDER-BASED VIOLENCE

Humanity continues to experience serious violations of human rights, and the recent critical events, like the COVID-19 pandemic and the war in Ukraine, seem to have directly or indirectly intensified the occurrence of violations of human rights like torture, enforced disappearances, human trafficking, gender-based violence and war crimes. Can analytical psychology make a significant contribution to the prevention, treatment, remedying such violations, from the individual level to the most macro level of socio-political systems ? I will support the thesis that the Jungian concept of soul has a special role in such an endeavour. My proposal is that when a social terrifying threat, like in the case of widespread social violence, is perceived at the social level, the functioning of the individual Self and society may change dramatically. In particular, both lose their containing function and are subjected to an unconscious massive collective pressure to align themselves to a specific kind of functioning that I call monolithic functioning. It is the splintering of what I call the reflective triangle, which is illustrated here, and has an effect on societal, groupal, interpersonal and intrapsychic levels. Some vignettes from a clinical case of a patient who suffered torture and gender-based violence are presented to illustrate how these human rights violations affect the three levels mentioned.

PSYCHOSOMATICS, SOMATIZATION, SOMATOFORM DISORDERS, OBJECT RELATIONS, WINNICOTT, THE FALSE SELF, DEFICIT PATHOLOGY, ALEXITHYMIA

In this article, the author investigates the wide variation in historical and contemporary understandings of somatization. The article explores the rewards of understanding somatization as a deficit pathology and proposes an integration of deficit pathology theory and Winnicott's theory of self to better understand the causes of somatization. The author postulates a link between the formation of a pathological false self and somatoform symptoms and draws on Killingmo's description of conflict and deficit pathology to integrate the defensive organization (false self) with the concept of deficit. The false self is conceptualized as a defensive organization that is born in a climate of deficit, including early childhood trauma. Therapeutic implications include a focus on experiencing meaning, working with alexithymia, and providing the client an opportunity to confront the painful reality of their unmet needs, in a safe and holding environment not afforded to them in childhood. The author outlines the therapeutic goal of moving toward a renewed sense of ‘equilibrium of self, where a person can freely and safely demonstrate vulnerability as well as meet their own needs. This in turn works to reduce the need for the protection of a pathological false self and the tightly bound somatoform symptomatology.

PSYCHOTHERAPIST, WOUNDED HEALER, TATTOO, GENDER, FEMINISM, TRAUMA, INTERPRETATIVE PHENOMENOLOGICAL ANALYSIS

This article considers the position of the female tattooed body within the context of the ‘caring professions’. Tattoos are increasingly popular within these workplaces, but a stigma persists. The limited psychoanalytic research on body modifications in the consulting room concludes that tattoos are either a superficial fashion choice or an indicator of deviance and/or self-harm. To initiate a conversation that can move away from the current pathologizing paradigm, I have considered the ways in which tattooing can be considered as a creative ‘working through’, distinct from an aggressive ‘acting out’. The research utilized an interpretative phenomenological analysis approach to examine the lived experiences of female therapists, with body modifications, in the consulting room. All participants focused on their tattoos as their significant body modification and experiences varied depending on the specifics of the client work, professional environment and beliefs about perceptions of tattoos from the wider population. Identified themes were: appearance of self in the consulting room; the perceived communication of one's inner world through inked skin and integration of the process of tattooing. Professionalism was emphasized as an integral consideration for revealing or concealing tattoos in the consulting room and specifically this was heightened in relation to being female.

ATTACHMENT, ENMESHMENT, PSYCHODYNAMIC CONSULTATION, HOMELESSNESS, HOMELESS COUPLES, UNHOUSED MINDS

Domestic violence is a prevalent public health concern, affecting millions worldwide. The presence of domestic violence affecting women and couples experiencing homelessness both continue to be underreported areas of clinical work and commissioning within the sector. This paper explores the difficulties of trying to house and contain unhoused couples with reference to the psychoanalytic ideas of attachment and the claustro-agoraphobic dilemma. The paper argues that more wrap-around support, such as temporary alternative housing options, are required to manage instances of domestic abuse and instances of attachment anxiety. Flexible options are also required to account for the likelihood that a couple may return to the streets when perpetrators are evicted based upon the implementation of blanket policies. The paper also attempts to offer some nuance into the complexities of relational dynamics, which are amplified by two unhoused minds coming into intimate contact with one another in front of a professional audience. The paper concludes with drawing attention to the lack of therapeutic support and lack of appetite to commission this to enable couples to explore the roles each partner can play when enmeshed in destructive forms of relating.

PSYCHOANALYSIS, PSYCHEDELIC THERAPY, TRAUMA, PTSD, PSYCHOTHERAPY, PSYCHEDELICS

The psychedelic state can be thought about as an interdependent intrapsychic, somatic, interpersonal and spiritual happening which encourages, perhaps both to the relief and dismay of those participating in the experience, the shocking and impressive emergence of one's unconscious desires and traumata's; a state which may be experienced as cathartic or healing, and as anxiety-provoking and confusing. Often, in clinical trials investigating psychedelics in mental health conditions, these go hand in hand. Amid a renewed, at times hyperbolic, interest in psychedelics as a potential treatment for mental ill health, significant gaps of knowledge remain. Additional studies exploring the impact of the extra-pharmacological factors and adjunct therapeutic models on treatment outcomes are needed. Drawing from psychoanalytic perspectives, this paper explores points of intersectionality between psychedelic therapy under investigation and psychoanalysis in the context of traumatic stress. To that end, the psychedelic state will be considered an attempt to make the unconscious conscious by immersing self in a bewildering waking-dream to better tolerate reality; immersing self in a wilful state of vulnerability, to develop trust in one's agency and capacity to trust others; immersing self in an indescribable experience to learn how to redescribe, to self and to others the traumatic past.

Sebastian Thrul  

Reading the material for the first time, a number of associations and affective responses well up in me: Maud—what a quaint, old-fashioned name, I think. It sounds antiquated and it brings to mind the image of a stereotypical spinster. The latter thought and the concomitant associations to (lack of) sexual intercourse and marriage are enriched by two pieces of information: the process revolved around questions of Maud's ‘engagement’ with it, with her analyst; and a striking discrepancy between her apparent ‘wish to make herself available’ in the pretreatment questionnaire and her withdrawn attitude in the actual treatment.

I feel the ambivalence between her wanting to engage, longing for intercourse and staying a safe, but lifeless distance in her analyst's story about the beginning of treatment. I learn that she tried to kill herself and sense my own curiosity rising, wanting to know more—what did she do? I imagine an attack on her own body with a knife, cutting herself open. I seem to remember an eminent psychoanalyst who made a point of using the German word ‘Selbstmord’ in conversation with patients, marking the violence against the self in a much clearer and more direct way than the technical ‘Suizid’. Both German words translate to the English ‘suicide’, but ‘Selbstmord’ combines the words ‘Selbst’ (self) and ‘Mord’ (murder) to the effect of more aggressive associations. I wonder what is omitted in the abstract description of Maud's suicide attempt. The question ‘Why not call a spade a spade?’ comes to mind. Maud appears to be both aggressive and violent so, there is frustration welling up in me now, and a forceful curiosity: I become impatient to know what she did to herself.

From the description, Maud seems to stumble into psychoanalytic treatment without being able to formulate a hope or wish for such an intensive and demanding process. It feels like she is passive in being sent to psychotherapy and consequently does not seem to care much about keeping to the frame. Is she just indifferent, or is she actually violent towards the frame, the agreed upon setting, the analyst? I find myself internally applauding the analyst's resolve ‘to show her how actively, unconsciously, she sought to break the connection with her objects’. Then again, I am puzzled by the remark that ‘She began to see how her regular work trips broke the link between us and with the work’. Having read just shortly before that her attendance was erratic even without the occasional work-related absence, it seems noteworthy that the recurrent breaking of the link is now attributed to the somewhat external factor of work. I feel an urge to point out that she herself breaks the link, not the work trips. I wonder why the analyst approaches her aggression with such ambivalence, and at times, caution.

Jan Hepburn  

This comprehensive book encompasses vast tracts of psychoanalytic theory and the work of several theoreticians on the subject of mourning and how it is metabolized. Meyerowitz promises ‘close-reading’ and ‘keen-eyed attention to detail’ (p. 8) of all the texts and this is done in a masterly fashion. Furthermore, he decided not to use his own clinical experiences to illustrate or exemplify the points, but to use literary texts to help ground the ideas, one short story in particular, which are woven throughout the book. Meyerowitz declares his position, which has been developed and digested over many years of thinking and clinical practice, as well as from his earlier career as an academic in literary studies and critical theory, from the outset. He links the failure of mourning—melancholia—with the fear of loss and thus the impossibility of metabolizing it. He notes that ‘all human experience is predicated on loss’ (p. 5). He also thinks that the processing required to manage loss mirrors the digestive process and that melancholia is a kind of psychic indigestion. This is the metaphor he uses throughout the book to hold it together and to help the reader to digest what is by any measure a substantial and rich meal.

The introduction, some 26 pages, sets all this out and more, as Meyerowitz expands on his understandings and describes how poetry and prose are used to both bring something to life and to help with this digestive process. The second part of the introduction delineates how the book is organized and what the reader can hope to find there. It is in this section that the ordinary reader, who might have been concerned that a book of this size without clinical examples could be rather challenging to digest, can be reassured. The writing style brings the various authors Meyerowitz is grappling with to life; the reader begins to see that Meyerowitz is in dialogue with these theoreticians and their theories. As the book progresses one can imagine that Meyerowitz and the authors are in the room talking together.

Introduction

When I first saw the clinical material for this commentary which amongst other things includes a clinician looking back over a period of time at work that took place at an earlier point in their career, it seemed fitting as this will be my last contribution as Clinical Commentaries Editor before I hand it on to my successor. I thought about how one of the great challenges in editing this section of the journal has been sourcing original clinical material, and, as any psychoanalytic author writing about a clinical experience is faced with, the multi-layered task of disguising the material. At the heart of this endeavour is choosing a name to take the place of the actual name of the patient. ‘What is in a name?’—this is far more complex than it might seem; names bring up so many associations as each of the writers below express in equally unique ways. For me, it evoked the Tennyson poem in which there are some parallels, including the theme of suicide and the elusive Maud whom the poem's narrator describes as ‘dead perfection’. All three commentaries, although drawing out different aspects of the patient—life, death, aggression, the ephemeral quality of a silent movie star and the sort of creativity that can only emanate from extreme conditions (a concentration camp) all evoke the sense of distance this patient creates and how hard it is for the patient to maintain contact with the analyst and with her own libidinal self. I would therefore like to thank the anonymous clinician whose clinical work has inspired these responses and as much as we may struggle to see the patient, we are also generously offered a glimpse of the clinician's experience which is so relevant here. In addition to this I would like to thank the authors of the three commentaries, both the current and former Editors, Gary Winship and Ann Scott, and my colleagues on the Board whose support and advice have been invaluable to me over the past few years.

ANALYTIC LISTENING, UNCONSCIOUS PROCESSES, LEARNING, PLAY, PAINTING, CREATIVITY

This paper explores how the process of learning to harness one's creativity in analytic listening can be analogous to the process of learning to do so in painting. It draws on clinical work with one client divided into two vignettes. The first describes the author's attempts to listen analytically by paying attention to form and content; narrative structure and use of language; and by paying attention to transference and countertransference communications. The second vignette explores what happened between therapist and client as the author had grown sufficiently confident to respond more intuitively to her client's communications. It describes how the process of becoming sufficiently familiar with theory was, paradoxically, what enabled her to respond to unconscious communications more loosely and creatively in the analytic encounter. It then explores what happened when she communicated this back to the client. The paper also describes how, as a result of the training and personal therapy, a parallel process of learning to let go and play was unfolding in the author's experience of painting. It concludes that learning to harness creativity in the therapeutic encounter can have an unexpected and welcome impact on the therapist's own artistic endeavours.

Juliet Rosenfeld  

As I read the story of Maud a character came to my mind; The Poor Little Rich Girl. Originally a 1913 Broadway play, in 1917 an eponymous silent movie came out. Gwendolyn is a child born to privilege, but neglected and forgotten by her parents she finds escape in fantasy and illusion. One day a careless nanny overdoses her with medicine and Gwendolyn's ensuing illness is what finally gets her parents' attention as she hovers between life and death. In her hazed delirium, Gwendolyn is able to conjure up a world of lonely lost children and her parents are finally forced to confront their selfish behaviour and consider the consequences of their careless parenting.

Maud too is a young woman apparently born to privilege (there was family money behind her), but unable to find emotional sustenance or connection with real people. Unlike little Gwendolyn (or maybe a grown-up Gwendolyn might have done so too), Maud's imaginative capacity has come to life in the shape of her writing. Maud has a book contract with a prominent publisher and part-time work too. Maud with a pen, keyboard or passport it seems is an imaginative, able person, capable of much, including presenting herself professionally, being punctual and meeting deadlines. And yet … the therapist's experience of her seems almost the opposite of this within the limits of the excerpt of the particular session we are given.

From the beginning, I wondered and continued to wonder: where are the parents, and how did Maud end up here? Despite the regular contact she has with them by phone, they seem completely absent and almost never to have existed—two lines are given to mother, father and a family described as ‘unremarkable’. This feels ambiguous given what the preceding paragraph has told us.

Just before treatment, Maud too had hovered between life and death after a suicide attempt. The intense therapy is suggested by her outpatient psychiatrist. Although both a psychiatrist and therapist are involved with Maud, and then the on/off boyfriend James, Maud remains an evanescent presence in the account of her treatment. As I read and reread, and reread her therapist's account of their work together, I wondered who on earth she was. Even now, writing about the clinical material, an empty feeling accompanies me as I type. Who was Maud? Where was Maud? Did Maud even really exist? Perhaps my reference to the silent film links to her grey shadowy presence. I could never hear her voice in my head.

In her author talk on World Book night 2022 (Crediton Library, nd), Gabriella Braun noted that although her original conception of this book was that it was for leaders of organizations, she quickly realized she wanted to write a book for everyone—a series of stories about people's lives at work, that illustrated the universal struggles that individuals and organizations experience. In this she has succeeded. This is a humane and generous book that attends to theoretical concepts but always keeps a light touch as it offers insights into the activities that for most of us makes up a third of waking life.

There is an intimacy in the book as we hear about the struggles of people who Braun has worked with, and this intimacy is echoed in the way she uses her own work history and autobiography to illustrate how much our early relationships and experiences impact and influence the ways we bring ourselves into work. The approach is therefore not of a distant and knowing consultant, but one of recognition that to be able to work meaningfully with the messiness of different work environments, one has to be prepared to feel first and use that counter-transference connection as essential information to offer ideas and insights to teams and individuals.

The book is divided into three sections: the first, ‘Human Nature at Work’, introduces what Braun calls ‘the fundamental of our minds’ (p. 8)—referencing key concepts such as Libido and Thanatos, the Unconscious, projective processes, defences and attachment. The second section, ‘Losing Ourselves’, pays attention to the pull of destructive processes and how these can take hold in systems and workplaces. The third and final section, ‘Finding Ourselves’, looks more towards the reparative capacities that can turn organizational difficulties around.

The book focuses on the role of the consultant to help teams, managers and leaders speak to one another, to attempt to look at what lies beneath the surface, unsaid, un-noticed, often denied or systematically and unconsciously avoided. In a world dominated by binaries of success and failure, truth and lies, winning and losing, and the imagined ‘outcomes’ of performance and productivity, this relational understanding of what makes for meaningful and effective working contexts is welcome. This, his most recent book, contributes to the now two-decade-old interdisciplinary attempt called neuropsychoanalysis to understand how neural activity in the brain transforms into psychic activity. Divided into nine chapters with titles inherently intriguing to psychoanalytic thinking such as ‘Self and narcissism’, ‘Dreams, depression and schizophrenia’, ‘Attachment and trauma’, and ‘Conscious and unconscious’, the book's main takeaway is that while it is true that certain parts of the brain certainly underpin specific functions (e.g., the occipital lobe for vision, the amygdala for fear), there is another dynamic, global aspect to brain function which depends on unique patterns of different kinds of brain wave activity.

You could say his aim in this book is to introduce another dimension to understanding the brain, so that space (i.e., where in the brain a function seems to reside) is augmented with an understanding of how the dynamics of time operate as an energetic and essential dimension of brain function as well. He is calling this lens through which he is looking spatiotemporal neuroscience, and each chapter explores how this new way of seeing can allow us to explore familiar concepts in a new way.

What he means by ‘spatial’ is how spontaneous activity in the brain occurs topographically through various interacting networks like the default-mode network, salience network, and central executive network, whose relationships seem to be modulated by the brain's global activity. The ‘temporal’ part refers to the brain's fluctuations or oscillations in various frequency ranges (in size order, largest to smallest, these are: gamma, alpha, beta, theta and delta waves) which, together, provide a certain temporal dynamic structure to different brain functions.

In his first chapter, ‘Self and narcissism’, Northoff draws on a concept of self he developed over a decade ago in which he argued that there are three layers of self, a bodily interoceptive self, an affective extero-proprioceptive self, and a cognitive, mental self. The interoceptive self is the most basic layer of the self. It is responsible for processing interoceptive stimuli from our own bodies and forms that part of which is known as the salience network, involving different areas of the brain. The next layer, the proprioceptive self, takes account of the environment and processes stimuli such as facial expression and tone of voice, as well as integrating the different sensory modalities, some of which filter up from the interoceptive self. Johnathan Sunley

Johnathan Sunley  

Who is Julia? Every time I read this clinical material I ask myself the same questions. What does she look like? Is she tall or short? Fair or dark? What does her voice sound like? How does she dress? Does she have a job? What are her hobbies? Sometimes when you hear from a colleague about a patient, you find yourself filling in details like these in your mind. Try as I might to picture Julia, I come up with practically nothing.

Of course, that might say more about me than it does about her. It is certainly not a reflection on the material itself, which I think powerfully conveys both the emptiness of Julia's existence and the demands that seeing her three times a week over a period of three years must have placed on her therapist. My understanding is that this is work that has ended, possibly some time ago. If that is the case, it is interesting that the therapist does not evaluate the work, saying to what extent they feel it helped Julia with her longstanding depression and low self-esteem. From the session presented, which takes place roughly half way through the treatment, it is hard to feel very optimistic. In taking this opportunity to write about Julia, I wonder if her therapist has been left with something they are still processing. Did they ever really get to know her? Who is Julia?

I want to begin with thinking about the way the session ends. For me the significance of this moment is underlined by the fact that this is also where the material as a whole concludes. Julia has been quiet, perhaps mulling over the last few exchanges with her therapist and the slightly greater closeness between them in the room. But now it is time to go. ‘When I announced the end of the session, she sat up, turned to look at me and smiled slightly, as she usually does, stood up and saw herself out. ’ This has the feeling of an interaction that is both highly charged and (apparently) without meaning—endings are always like this. To my mind this suggests an experience frozen in time, or what Zabriskie (1997) calls ‘frozen accidents’. These are one-off events that go on forever. ‘Present collapses into past, and one long psychological instant reverberates across decades. We may feel numb, as if in suspended timelessness—or frenzied in intensified no-timeness until meaning comes and one is released into ongoing time’ (Zabriskie, 1997, p. 37).

Ann Scott  

We meet Julia 15 months into a three-year, intensive psychoanalytic psychotherapy. The clinician's succinct presentation of the case suggests that by now, enough of a therapeutic alliance has been established for Julia to become ‘more curious about her feelings’, after a ‘cautious’ first year. There is a background of unhappily married parents: mother frighteningly volatile, though at times gentle; father much loved by the patient but seemingly ineffectual and frequently absent. There is a series of what may have been rather short-lived relationships with men, each evolving into a friendship when the relationship ended. It seems that ‘the void’ is always waiting in the wings for Julia, and fear of it may keep her in a relationship/friendship that she would otherwise choose to end. Importantly, we are told that Julia frequently feels angry, and that in the countertransference the therapist is ‘more in touch’ with Julia's feelings of emptiness and loneliness than with her anger.

This clinical picture brought a number of possibilities to my mind. Depression and low self-esteem, we are told, have brought Julia to treatment. We may assume that a containing warmth could never be relied on in childhood and this may have led, defensively, to the patient's very muted response to her objects. The therapist aptly notes the dismissive use to which ‘anyway’ is put by the patient; other expressions probably serve a similar function: ‘it was silly really’ or ‘I knew it was ridiculous’ or ‘according to my friend, he was very upset’, or ‘apparently he was also upset’ . All seem designed to diminish salience, perhaps to keep emotion out of the room, and out of the patient's own mind. Nevertheless, there are glimpses of a more vital conflict—the dynamic of attraction/repulsion that the therapist mentions in relation to the patient's choice of lovers—which we would expect to see represented, however fleetingly, in the treatment. With this dynamic in mind, my assumption is that the patient, throughout the session, is subtly moving towards and away from her therapist. This could perhaps have been explored more explicitly; had it been— and with a more sustained emphasis on the here-and-now of the session—we might have seen something of the anger in the countertransference that the therapist says he/she was less in touch with.

As I embarked on reading this selection of past papers by Margaret Rustin, I set about it in the way I have often used in book reviews—copying particularly inspiring or insightful phrases into a document so I could refer to them or quote them in the review to come. Before I had got very far into the book, I realized that I was rapidly accumulating a huge collection of beautiful examples of observational acuity, thoughtful analysis, deep empathy and wisdom. My document was becoming full and lengthy—I was in danger of copying and pasting most of the book! The emphasis moved to being on what to leave out rather than what to include. I will endeavour in this review to capture what seem to be the most valuable contributions but am aware that I will not be able to do it justice.

Rustin manages in every part of this book to demonstrate her capacity to ‘integrate feeling and thinking’ in a way that facilitates a deep and compassionate engagement with all her patients and their parents, carers and professional networks. She has so much to offer, yet never seems to lose her sense that it is she who has the ‘privilege of undertaking clinical work with children and adolescents’ (p. xiv) from which she goes on learning during decades of practice.

As some of the psychoanalytic world still struggles to give due weight to psychosocial factors in our patients’ difficulties, Rustin presents us with both a straightforwardly sensible and a subtle awareness of the complexity of the interactions between a child's internal world and their external world. She is consistently and impressively even-handed in her appreciation both of the damage parents can do to their children and the intense pressures on families and the unprocessed pain and anxiety which constrict the parents’ capacity for care and love. Likewise, she has some powerful comments to make about the failings in social care, fostering arrangements and residential units, but always tempers these with a countervailing empathy with the difficulties facing professionals, the way in which projective processes interfere with the functioning of networks, and a stress on the systemic underfunding of services which lead otherwise well meaning people to fall short in their roles.

The quality of the clinical encounter with Julia comes across clearly despite the omission of much detail for reasons of confidentiality. I was impressed by the 635 therapist's awareness of their own affective responses (King, 1978) and the respect for silences. The work in the clinician's mind, particularly of receptivity, listening and containment is sensitive and clear.

It is interesting that Julia, troubled since childhood, seeks help in her late 40s. Why at this point? Why have her longstanding depression and low self-esteem become more unbearable? Perhaps she fears being on her own for the rest of her life? She seems aware of her pattern of relating. Does Julia also feel cut off and despairing about herself? I wondered about her disturbed, rather restricted and futile relationship with self and the other.

As the youngest of three children with a mother whom she experienced as changeable, sometimes attuned, and other times terrifying, Julia experienced her father as more stable and capable of intimacy. However, he was often absent and passive to the point of being weak in terms of protecting Julia and her siblings from her mother's disturbance. We know nothing more about the nature of Julia's relationships with her older siblings, other than the described family dynamics of hostility, criticism, conditional love and rivalries, nor do we know much about the patient's life beyond her immediate family. We do not know about relationships with other children, teachers, and her functioning at school, including her capacity to learn and play. What is striking is the unhappiness of the parental couple signifying a relative lack of creative intercourse and the poignant early memory, presumably a screen memory of Julia as a small girl standing in the window of her bedroom, crying as she watched her father driving away on his business trip without kissing her goodbye. To me, this seemed especially painful: the missing caress, the somatic communication, experience of touch and act of love which might have helped little Julia to keep the loving aspects of her father in mind. One sees an avoidance of strong feelings on the part of the paternal object: love, sadness, regret, guilt, anger, helplessness, and Julia seems to have identified with and internalized this defensive manoeuvre.

Katya Orrell  

Introduction

In clinical commentary 46 we hear about a patient, a woman, emotionally deprived in childhood, whom our first commentator tells us longs for intimacy but who also avoids it. All three commentators write about this lack and its effects, which, over time, becomes a presence that fills the patient's life and takes precedence in relationships. This, we learn, appears to hinge symbolically on a kiss, or rather the absence of a kiss, the kiss of a parent and its accompanying legacy. We know there are many different forms and meanings a kiss may take, including as our first commentator introduces, the theme of betrayal, which also brings to mind the kiss of Judas. In the case of the patient it is the missing kiss that has the devastating effect, which our second commentator describes as a lack of ‘somatic communication’, reminding us how the physical sensation of touch is necessary to keep good objects alive in a patient's mind. One only needs to watch parents saying goodbye at a school gate to see that for a young child, a kiss marks both love and affection but that it is also the moment of release, a gesture offering the child independence, signifying a vital confidence that the child (and parent) can survive the separation. Another example, are children growing up in boarding schools who may defend against this emotional deprivation via the excitement of late night dormitory high jinks, but without a good night kiss something elemental is missing, the night is left open and unsafe, sometimes literally. When a child falls over and scrapes their knee it is not the plaster or the antiseptic that heals but more often than not it is the kiss, as we read in our third commentator's description of the patient's ‘muted response’ to her objects as a result of this absent kiss and what is left behind. The lasting effect this has on the patient is unanimously felt and understood by all three commentators as we discover below. Finally, I would like to thank the clinician who has generated such a rich combination of thoughts and ideas through sharing their material. It is not an easy task and as always I am impressed by the care and sensitivity that goes into this very considered piece of writing.

This recently published Tavistock Clinic Series book is an engaging, comprehensive, much-needed and ground-breaking publication edited by Jo Stubley and Linda Young. It has been deservedly nominated for a Gradiva Award, which showcases the best works that advance psychoanalysis.

Clinicians in the second generation of the Trauma Service have been building on Caroline Garland's (1998) work by moving it into the territory of complex trauma, anchoring it in neuroscience and attachment theories, and acknowledging the narrowness of Cartesian dualism splitting the mind from the body. They have been responding to the needs of various groups of patients presenting to the service, developing their expertise in general principles and in specific areas. This work required clinicians to be creative and adapt the psychoanalytic technique, as well as embrace innovative interventions incorporating the mind and the body, resulting in a truly holistic approach which places relationships at the heart of the work. Confidence and joy in clinical work is abundant through the book, and one of its biggest assets—despite the distressing nature of patients’ stories—is that it is always underpinned by the humility of the clinicians. A stance of curiosity, sensitivity and kindness is paramount across all chapters and anchored in the robust conceptual framework. The importance of not working in isolation and connection to others is highlighted, acknowledging the weight of work with trauma and the potential for vicarious traumatization. This work can get caught up in repetition compulsion patterns and is prone to re-enactments which serve the purpose of communication, moving the work forward. To disentangle an often complex web of these dynamics—a space for reflection in the context of relationships with others—is vital. The Tavistock Trauma Service certainly comes across as taking this seriously, including the innovative approach described in the chapter ‘Writing Trauma’.

Even the book cover lithograph by trauma course administrator Billie Joseph illustrates the centrality of relationships in the service. The interior of the double aspect staircase in the Tavistock building suggests warmth, shelter and a place of safety in the otherwise stark, black and white world outside. The cover is apt because working with complex trauma can be stark, and the pull towards black and white thinking is strong, highlighting the importance of finding a thinking space where it can be processed.

PSYCHOTHERAPY, ONLINE THERAPY, COVID-19, THERAPEUTIC ALLIANCE, SHARED CRISIS

The objective of this study was to capture therapists' experiences of delivering therapy throughout the COVID-19 pandemic and how this experience impacted therapeutic alliance. Quantitative and qualitative analyses were conducted on the responses to three surveys distributed to all UKCP members. The qualitative and quantitative analyses found significant variability in therapists' feelings regarding the transition to online therapy, with overall perceptions continuing to be divided similarly throughout the nine months surveyed. While qualitative data highlighted positive perceptions of online therapy for some, quantitative results showed that most did not find online therapy to be as effective as face-to-face therapy. The pandemic and subsequent shift to online work had significant implications for therapists, including navigating unfamiliar changes to the therapeutic space resulting from experiencing a shared crisis, and holding the frame in relation to boundaries of safety. In the wake of the pandemic, as things shift increasingly towards a hybrid model of delivering therapy, it is important to reflect on what can be learned from this transition and how this influences future therapeutic practices.

Readers of this journal may well be familiar with Sigmund Freud's claim that we are driven by a death instinct to repeat traumatic and other experiences in the psychological form afforded by memories and dreams. Readers may be less familiar, like me, with the related claim made by the philosopher Jacques Derrida regarding the compulsion to memorialize ourselves and others in written and other archival form.

Now, thanks to psychotherapist Tara Blake's book, Archive Fevers, I know more about Derrida's claim. This is due to Blake illustrating it in terms of an engaging email correspondence between a fictional psychotherapist Hannah and her patient Scarlett beginning in early June 1997 when Scarlett's work takes her to the archive of the anthropologist Margaret Mead in Washington DC.

PSYCHOANALYTIC THEORY, PSYCHIC RETREAT, OVERVALUED IDEAS, CONSPIRACY THEORIES, REPTILIAN CONSPIRACY

This paper investigates whether conspiracy theories arising during the COVID-19 pandemic are linked to early trauma or a specific organization of the mind. Using the Reptilian conspiracy theory as an example, the paper proposes that belief in conspiracy theories can activate unresolved memories of trauma and serve as a mediator between the psyche and intrusive content. Classic psychoanalytic concepts, as well as more modern ideas from Britton and Steiner, are explored to understand the role of early trauma and inner object relations dynamics in the development of Belief in Reptilian Conspiracy Theories (BiCT). The concept of après-coup is introduced to explain how newer responses to familiar psychic experiences may shape beliefs in conspiracies. Additionally, the paper proposes that belief in conspiracy theories can function as a psychic retreat. Two clinical cases are presented to illustrate these ideas while maintaining anonymity.

Neil Morgan  

What are our geographical boundaries for reading? Mostly we read British analysts, perhaps going across the Channel if we are Francophiles. But do we read more widely, say from Scandinavia, South America, and so on? The author of this book is a training analyst from the vibrant Israeli Psychoanalytical Society. He has written an interesting and important book. The subtitle is Beyond the Spectrum in Psychoanalysis. It brings to mind, historically, André Green's address to the IPA conference in London, some time back (in 1975) about broadening the spectrum of psychoanalysis, beyond the neurotic spectrum, and his work on the Negative.

We are used to thinking about psychic representation, and almost taking it for granted. Nevertheless, Bergstein's focus throughout this significant and thought- provoking text is on how experience and affect does or does not get into representation. This is what he means by the infra and ultraviolet spectrum, metaphorically, that he wants to draw our attention to—the realm of invisible, unverbalizable psychic reality for the patient. If the patient cannot verbalize his experience, how can we hear, or ‘see’ it?

The clinical work described in the book concerns a different sort of unconscious to the one we are used to thinking about and dealing with. It is not the robustly represented repressed unconscious that is amenable to classical analytic interpretation. Levine, Read and Scarfone (2013), Mitrani (1996, 2001) and Eekoff (2019, 2022) have written about such presentation. The patients that each of these authors describes are forced to present, rather than represent their psychic life. The analyst, via their counter transference, has to turn the patient's void/negative into a positive representable reality.

Bergstein expands on Bion's question ‘Can we make some extension of our mental capacity to take in a little bit more of the … invisible aspects of the spectrum’ (p. 55)—that is beyond the verbally communicable. One of the strengths of the book is how it combines a good balance of theoretical discussion with detailed work from Bergstein's encounters with his patients, which he uses to illustrate his argument.

Kristina Schellinski  

Understanding the great works of James Joyce is a formidable challenge, as is understanding the inner world of a replacement child, attested to by many a therapist's difficulties in diagnosing the condition in adult patients. Mary Adams is 251 looking at two principal works of Joyce, namely Ulysses and Finnegans Wake, giving full consideration to James Joyce being born a year after the death of his brother, ‘his parents were still grieving’ (p. 1). A replacement child is one born to replace a sibling or given or taking on such a role later on. The replacement child syndrome can entail guilt and grief, identity and self-esteem issues, attachment and relational problems, and a preoccupation with life and death issues.

Joyce's father felt that his son James had ‘usurped the cot of his deceased elder brother. This feeling that his new son was a substitute was never to be admitted’ (Adams citing Jackson and Costello biographers of James Joyce, 1977, p. 39).

Mary Adams is a Kleinian psychoanalyst, now retired, with decades of clinical experience and a great and insightful passion for literature, especially James Joyce. Her book is delightful to read and well researched, full of citations and references, with poignant quotes from his works, and her first-hand understanding of working with two adult replacement children in her practice. In an appendix, Adams lists famous replacement children from the arts, from Shakespeare and William Blake to Goethe and Kollwitz, Ibsen, Kafka, Yeats; from Beethoven to Mahler, Matisse, van Gogh and Dali, the latter two are some of the most researched replacement children. Self-examination and creative expression are two ways for a replacement child to reconnect with the true, original life force within. In accessing the unconscious, a new sense of self can be gleaned; Adams writes, Joyce finishes Finnegans Wake as ‘a legitimate son’ (p. 103), in Joyce's original way of writing we can also find his self-examination.

As I am more knowledgeable on the replacement child condition than with respect to the work of James Joyce, I will focus on replacement child aspects in the hope that colleagues as well as those intimate with James Joyce will find this adding to the rich tapestry of our understanding of Joyce's works and the human soul in general.

America became the refuge for European analysts who had been disinherited and exiled by the Nazis. Even before, and as far back as the time after World War I, a small group of analysts had visited Vienna and returned with enthusiasm after meeting Freud and learning of the promise of a new treatment for mental illness. One of those fleeing Europe was the Russian Gregory Zilboorg who would eventually make his own mark in psychoanalytic history. He had tremendous intellect, and his commanding presence and countenance was hard to discount. His gift of languages mixed easily with lecturing and teaching. His love of stage, any stage, including the stage of psychoanalysis, combined with his love of lecturing, made time with him memorable. His work on suicide is noteworthy but his major contribution may be his work on the History of Medical Psychology (1941) as well as his editing of the volume celebrating the centenary of the American Psychiatric Association in 1944, One Hundred Years of American Psychiatry. Overall, Zilboorg could be considered the one who combined history, psychiatry and psychoanalysis to form a broader framework of humanistic theory in his writings.

This two-volume biography of Gregory Zilboorg, written by his daughter, a distinguished literary and historical scholar, is nothing short of an extraordinarily intimate and well researched reflective—the story of one man's personal and professional development and life-long contributions to medicine, drama, psychology and psychoanalysis. The author has painstakingly researched her family's archives, most were collected and catalogued by her mother, and has produced a two-volume offering that is scholarly yet reads like a novel. Through diaries and other writings, we are privy to Zilboorg's thoughts as he navigates his life, from early childhood to the Russian Revolution, his early education, his interest in poetry and drama, his talent for languages, and the move to America where he clashes with early psychoanalytic giants, and where he finally finds professional success, personal happiness and spirituality. This biography is sophisticated in its style and is an admirably forthright account of Zilboorg's life. The author even discusses the ‘scandals’ and does so with professionalism and objectivity, always offering the reader published and unpublished data for support. It is most difficult to put aside, and no doubt will never become out-of-date. It is a one-of-a-kind book.
